Family Name: Brazil's Adaptation Climate Plan: Thematic Plan for the Ocean and Coastal Zone
Family Summary:
Brazil’s Thematic Plan for Ocean and Coastal Zones aims to increase the resilience of coastal communities, marine ecosystems, and ocean-based economic activities by addressing climate risks such as sea-level rise, coastal erosion, ocean warming, and extreme weather events through integrated adaptation and ecosystem-based management. The main goals are:

  • Strengthen the adaptive capacity of coastal and marine systems to climate change impacts.
  • Support the resilience of coastal populations and ocean-dependent economic sectors through sustainable and climate-informed adaptation measures.
  • Reduce vulnerabilities associated with sea-level rise, coastal erosion, flooding, ocean warming, acidification, and extreme events.
  • Integrate climate adaptation into coastal and marine planning, governance, and territorial management.
  • Protect, conserve, and restore coastal and marine ecosystems that provide climate resilience and ecosystem services.

Family Name: Brazil's Adaptation Climate Plan: Thematic Plan for Traditional Peoples and Communities
Family Summary:
Brazil’s Thematic Plan for IndigenousTraditional Peoples and Communities aims to support the presence of Traditional Peoples in their traditional territories is an essential condition, both for the preservation of their ways of life and to prevent changes in land use from further exacerbating the situation of climate change that is already underway. Grounded on ther right to live in peace, safety, and good health, and to enjoy the integrity of the ecosystems they inhabit, with a good quality of life and economic prosperity, the plan seeks to ensure:

Family Name: Clean electrification roadmap
Family Summary:
This roadmap outlines some steps that the UK is taking in clean electrification, in order to strengthen energy security, competitiveness and affordability; create green growth and jobs; and reduce emissions. The three priorities are to modernise the electricity system; help all households and businesses switch to fair, affordable and clean electricity, bringing down costs and supporting the most vulnerable; and build the skills and supply chains needed for delivery. Internationally, the UK will coordinate support with countries accelerating transition planning, as the co-chair of Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels Santa Marta workstream 1.

To modernise the electricity system, the UK is installing Dynamic Line Ratings (DLR) technology to carry electricity more safely and increase circuit capability; pioneering a place-based approach to electricity network planning; utilising legislation and technical standards, e.g. on smart tariffs, smart charging and home batteries; and reducing energy costs.

To help households and businesses electrify, there are loans to support home electrification and increased heat pump uptake; a new building standard; improved energy efficiency standards; switches to electric transport through grants and the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate; and exemptions from policy and capacity costs for energy-intensive industries.

To enable the transition with skills and the supply chain, there are the Clean Energy Jobs Plan and Industries Sector Plan, with investment towards frontier clean energy industries, increased trade union representation, and government grants and procurement to promote workforce criteria.
Document Title: Clean electrification roadmap

Family Name: Germany's Roadmap for Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels
Family Summary:
This Roadmap outlines Germany's commitment to transition away from fossil fuels no later than 2045. It was developed in the context of the Paris Agreement, Decision 1/CMA.5 of the first Global Stocktake, which calls for a just, orderly and equitable transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems to reach net zero by 2050, and European Union commitments, including the binding 90% emissions reduction target for 2040 under the European Climate Law. It is anchored in the Federal Climate Action Act, which sets legally binding reductions of at least 65% by 2030 and 88% by 2040 and net greenhouse gas neutrality by 2045, and in the 2026 Climate Action Programme, whose 67 measures underpin the sectoral strategies. These cover energy, transport, buildings and industry, supported by carbon pricing, research and innovation, social measures and international cooperation.

The Roadmap sets out how Germany will reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels through the rapid expansion of renewables (at least 80% of electricity by 2030), electrification, and the use of climate-neutral fuels where direct electrification is not yet viable. It confirms the legal phase-out of coal-fired power generation by 2038, with 2035 under consideration. It also provides for hydrogen-ready gas plants operating climate-neutrally by 2045, a switch to climate-neutral heating fuels from 2045, and EU emissions trading covering about 85% of national emissions. Internationally, Germany supports the transition through the Powering Past Coal Alliance, Just Energy Transition Partnerships, bilateral energy partnerships and €11.8 billion in climate finance in 2024. The Roadmap does not set separate end dates for oil and gas, and it recognises that fossil fuels will remain in use during a transitional period
Document Title: Germany's Roadmap for Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels

Family Name: Resolution No. 994 on the approval of rules for carbon credit transactions via the Reserve Account
Family Summary:
This Resolution sets out the rules for an authorised operator to conduct transactions with carbon credits through the reserve account. Carbon credits shall be credited to the reserve account upon issuance into circulation and, where required, in climate projects involving a risk of greenhouse gas release. Carbon credits held in the reserve account cannot be sold, pledged, encumbered, or seized. Carbon credits may be moved from the reserve account only after a report on the implementation of climate projects containing verified results of emissions reductions and project performance.

This reserve account safeguards climate projects with reversal risks, such as for carbon capture and storage. The rules will be in effect from 1 March 2027 to 1 March 2033, a period of six years.
Document Title: Resolution No. 994 on the approval of rules for carbon credit transactions via the Reserve Account

Family Name: National Transport Systems Plan 2026-2037 (Transport 12 Plan)
Family Summary:
Finland's Transport 12 Plan states GHG reduction within its broader energy-efficiency and sustainability goals. Domestic transport emissions stood at roughly 9.7 Mt CO2-eq in 2024 (about 4% higher than 2023, but down 26% since 2005), and Finland's binding EU effort-sharing target requires a 50% cut versus 2005 levels by 2030, with transport being the largest emitting sector within that target (about 38% being 96% of it from road transport). The Transport 12 Plan focuses on measures such as: promoting alternative-fuel distribution infrastructure (EV charging, hydrogen), supporting continued electrification of passenger and heavy vehicle fleets, growing the renewable/biofuel blending share in liquid fuels, funding public transport and walking/cycling infrastructure especially in the seven largest urban regions, and improving efficiency of the existing network.

However, the report also flags that several government-program measures work against these goals: a reduced renewable fuel distribution obligation, lower fuel taxes, higher VAT on public transport, and cuts to walking/cycling investment funding.
Document Title: National Transport Systems Plan 2026-2037 (Transport 12 Plan)

Family Name: Farming Roadmap 2050: Growing England’s Future
Family Summary: The Farming Roadmap 2050 treats climate and nature as part of productive farming rather than a trade-off, committing to maintain domestic food production at least at current levels while restoring biodiversity, improving water and air quality and cutting emissions. Agriculture produced about 12% of UK greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 and is on track to become the highest-emitting sector by 2050, so the Climate Change Committee's advice implies a fall of around 45% by 2050 against 2022 levels. The roadmap responds with a sector-wide emissions conversation in 2026, a Food and Farming Decarbonisation Plan, research into methane-suppressing feed and low-emission livestock systems, £1bn for tree planting and £85m for peatland restoration. On adaptation, it plans for at least 2°C of warming by 2050, with a fourth National Adaptation Programme in 2028, at least £300m for natural flood management (2026 to 2036), and measures on drought, water storage and wildfire risk. On nature, it points to statutory targets to halt species decline by 2030, restore or create 500,000 hectares of wildlife-rich habitat by 2042 (250,000 by 2030), and double the number of farms providing year-round wildlife resources by 2030.
Document Title: Farming Roadmap 2050: Growing England’s Future

Family Name: Decree of the Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM) No. 257.K/EK.01/MEM.E/2026 on Biodiesel
Family Summary: This Decree mandates the mixing of 50% biodiesel into all types of diesel fuel. Otherwise, petroleum and biofuel entities that fail to fulfil their obligations of blending and supply will be subject to administrative sanctions in the form of a written warning, temporary suspension and/or revocation of business licences. The implementation shall be evaluated by the Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources every three months.
Document Title: Decree of the Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM) No. 257.K/EK.01/MEM.E/2026 on Biodiesel

Family Name: Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26)
Family Summary: The Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) is an environmental land-management scheme for farmers and land managers in England, providing payments for actions that support environmental protection, sustainable food production and farm productivity. SFI26 offers 71 actions covering areas such as soil health, biodiversity, grassland and water management, with most actions lasting three years and payments generally made quarterly. Key changes from SFI24 include a minimum of 3 hectares of agricultural land, a £100,000 annual agreement value limit per farm business, one SFI26 agreement per farm business, removal of the SFI management payment, and the replacement of five-year actions with predominantly three-year actions. Applications for SFI26 closed in September 2026.

Family Name: France's Roadmap for Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels
Family Summary:
This Roadmap outlines France's commitment to transition away from fossil fuels. It was developed in the context of the Paris Agreement, Decision 1/CMA.5 on the outcomes of the first Global Stocktake to "[transition] away from fossil fuels, away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly and equitable manner, accelerating action in this critical decade, so as to achieve net zero by 2050 in keeping with the science", and European Union commitments to ensure that the European energy sector becomes largely free of fossil fuels.

While this Roadmap does not present new pledges, it brings existing climate and energy policies and targets under one umbrella with an explicit goal to transition away from fossil fuels. This Roadmap refers to the National Low Carbon Strategy (SNBC) and the Multiannual Energy Planning (PPE) for the following targets:

  • End-of-consumption targets for coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and fossil gas by 2050;
  • Close the last two coal-fired power plants by 2027.

This Roadmap also refers to National Plan for the Electrification of End-Uses (23 April 2026), which contains measures to reduce France's dependence on hydrocarbons across the sectors of transport, buildings, industry and small-scale manufacturing. In addition, the Roadmap refers to France's role in co-chairing the Coal Transition Commission launched at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, alongside Indonesia, as well as other coalitions and involvement in international climate finance.
Document Title: Feuille de route de la France pour une sortie progressive des énergies fossiles

Family Name: Transformation, Recovery and Resilience Plan (PTRR)
Family Summary:
This Plan is the plan to rebuild and recover from the losses caused by storms, to prepare the country to face climate events and other extreme risks, and to improve emergency response capabilities and support for the community at these moments. 

This plan allocates an overall sum of 22.6 billion euros, between national public funding, (37%), private funding (34%), and European funds (19%). Measures include a mandatory home insurance scheme linked to a national natural catastrophe and earthquake fund, upgrades to the emergency communications system, direct mobile phone alerts, and investments in energy, water, cybersecurity, and emergency accommodation infrastructure. There will also be a A new Calamity Law to regulate support in instances of emergency.
Document Title: Transformation, Recovery and Resilience Plan (PTRR)

Family Name: National Plan for the Electrification of End-Uses
Family Summary:
The plan for the electrification of uses is divided into 22 measures and targets the sectors that are currently the most reliant on fossil fuels: transport, buildings, industry and small-scale manufacturing. The measures include: -

In residential and commercial buildings:

  • By the end of 2026, it will no longer be possible to install gas boilers in new buildings. At the same time, public aid for private individuals will further support the replacement of gas and fuel oil boilers by heat pumps.
  • Two million social housing units will have to phase out gas by 2050.
  • The installation of 1 million heat pumps per year by 2030.

In transport sector:

  • The Government has set a target that two out of three new cars will be electric by 2030.
  • This strategy is accompanied by an industrial objective: French manufacturers will have to reach 400,000 electric vehicles produced per year from 2027, then 1 million by 2030. (Five years ago, no electric cars or batteries were produced in France.) The aim is to ensure that reduced dependence on oil does not translate into new dependence on imported vehicles.
  • For modest households, social EV leasing (cars with moderate monthly payments) will resume in June with 50,000 additional electric vehicles. A new system is also planned for key the middle-class workers, including home care workers, caregivers, nurses, craftsmen, employees and public servants, with 50,000 additional subsidized electric vehicles from 2026.

For companies, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the Government is introducing a support scheme. The government also aims to accelerate the decarbonisation of large industrial and agri-food sites. Artisans and retailers are also supported for electrification of work equipment.
Document Title: Electrification Plan

Family Name: National Climate Market Policy
Family Summary:
The overarching goal and vision of this Policy is to set out a structured framework that catalyses cost-effective climate action through a high-integrity, inclusive carbon market that accelerates national decarbonisation goals while delivering sustainable development co-benefits. The guiding principles are common but differentiated responsibility and respective capabilities; just and equitable transition; whole of society and national approach; and integrated and multi-sectoral solutions.

The Policy introduces a National Marginal Abatement Cost Curve, which ranks decarbonisation solutions based on the affordability of abating one tonne of emissions, to assess which types of projects are suitable for international agreements. Low-cost abatement options are prioritised for domestic mitigation, while higher-cost and hard-to-abate measures are most suitable for international cooperation under Article 6. Cost-effective solutions include energy-efficiency improvements, renewable-energy deployment, and waste management measures. Higher-cost abatement options include carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) and large-scale nature-based solutions.
Document Title: National Climate Market Policy

Family Name: National Carbon Market Policy
Family Summary:
The National Carbon Market Policy establishes a credible, transparent, and robust national framework for carbon market operations. It is designed to operationalise the Paris Agreement at a domestic level, helping Malaysia transition toward a low-carbon economy while achieving its climate targets. It provides policy guidance for the buyers and sellers of carbon credits generated from Malaysian carbon projects for three main compliance usage, i.e, NDC achievement, other international mitigation purposes (OIMP), and offset use for domestic compliance.

Key pillars of the policy:

The framework is structured around four core pillars:

Pillar 1: Implementation of a high-integrity carbon market - Focuses on generating verifiable, high-quality offsets and steering international participation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to safeguard national interests and prevent double counting.

Pillar 2: Driving a conducive carbon market ecosystem and infrastructure - Outlines the digital, technical, and regulatory infrastructure required, including the establishment of an integrated National Carbon Registry and a standardized Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) framework.

Pillar 3: Catalysing and accelerating carbon credit trading - Aims to reduce market entry friction by streamlining trading processes, improving project bankability, mobilizing public/private finance, and launching targeted incentive schemes.

Pillar 4: Complementing sectoral decarbonisation actions at domestic and international levels - Focuses on integrating carbon markets with potential Carbon Pricing Instruments (CPIs) (such as a future carbon tax or emissions trading scheme), ensuring sub-national readiness, and aligning with global trading measures.

Key core mechanisms

Paris Agreement Article 6 Alignment - Malaysia aligns its international trading with the rules of the Paris Agreement.

1. Article 6.2 and 6.4: Direct policy guidance is established for utilizing cooperative approaches and the centralized Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) to achieve carbon market obligations securely.

2. Corresponding adjustments (CA): Mandatory accounting rules are put in place to add or subtract mitigation outcomes between seller and buyer countries to avoid double counting.

3. Other International Mitigation Purposes (OIMP): The policy sets up authorization mechanisms for sector-specific international schemes, most notably CORSIA for international aviation, which becomes mandatory in 2027.

The Marginal Abatement Cost (MAC) Curve -The policy utilizes a National MAC Curve as an evidence-based tool to prioritize climate action.

1. Abatement potential: Assesses an overall emission-reduction potential of 56 MtCO2e in 2030 across more than 120 measures in six key sectors.

2. Domestic vs. international split: Approximately 70% (39 MtCO2e) consists of negative or low-cost options (e.g., energy efficiency, solar) reserved for domestic mitigation targets. The remaining 30% (17 MtCO2e) comprises high-cost, hard-to-abate measures (e.g., CCUS, hydrogen) that are deemed most suitable for international finance via Article 6.

Government crediting programmes - The operational market mechanism starts with a focus on forestry-based carbon credits through the Forest Carbon Offset (FCO) framework, reflecting Malaysia's distinct state-level land jurisdictions. Future sector expansions (e.g., waste, energy, transport) will be evaluated over time based on infrastructure readiness.

Policy enablers and delivery - To ensure institutional readiness, the policy lays out five cross-cutting enablers.

1. Legislation: Anchored by the upcoming National Climate Change Act to provide overriding legal authority.

2. Governance: Positioned under NRES as the Designated National Authority (DNA) and the Jawatankuasa Dekarbonisasi Kebangsaan (JDK) to bridge federal-state coordination.

3. Human Capital: Specialized capacity building, certification streams, and upskilling for project developers and frontline communities.

4. Strategic Resource Mobilization: Fulfilling the international share-of-proceeds obligations and evaluating funding structures for digital registries.

5. CEPA Framework: A Communication, Education, and Public Awareness framework aimed at reducing public misinformation, promoting youth climate leadership, and maintaining culturally sensitive dialogue with Indigenous communities regarding benefit-sharing.

Validation and Verification Body

The policy states that the government will maintain a public list of accredited VVBs authorised to operate within the national carbon market, and will provide clear information on the applicable accreditation frameworks and recognised standards required for validation and verification activities.

Recognition of methodologies by regulation

The policy explicitly recognizes and integrates independent international standards like Gold Standard, Verra, PACM, and JCM into its market architecture.

Registration of the PD or project with the national registry for VCM and Article 6

For VCM, registration is highly encouraged, but conditionally mandatory depending on the developer's intent, but is mandatory if it intends to seek Article 6 authorisation. While for Article projects, it is mandatory.

Approval for listing, issuance, trade, authorisation and corresponding adjustment

The regulation mandates government approval for listing, issuance, trade, and authorization.

Transfer of credits to registry after issuance and CA

Credits need to be admitted or reflected in the national registry immediately after issuance. Once a standard operator successfully processes a request for issuance, the resulting units are structurally recorded within the Transaction Registry to enable secure tracking, price discovery, and visibility across approved sales channels. The credits must interface directly with the national registry for a corresponding adjustment to occur.

Family Name: National Plan for Disaster Risk Reduction 2025-2029 (PNRRD)
Family Summary:
The National Disaster Risk Reduction Plan (PNRRD) 2025-2029 guides public policies on comprehensive risk management. It outlines the goals and objectives of programs, as well as actions aimed at reducing existing risks in order to protect people and their property. Its formulation involves the identification, analysis, and management of the causal factors of emergencies and disasters, with the objective of reducing exposure to hazards, decreasing the vulnerability of the population, and improving preparedness for adverse events. It establishes the multi-year strategic guidelines and goals that govern the National System for Comprehensive Risk Management and Civil Protection (SINAGIR), created by Law No. 27,287.

The priorities of the PNRRD 2025-2029 are:

  • Understanding disaster risk.
  • Strengthen governance of disaster risk management.
  • Increase disaster preparedness in order to provide an effective response.
  • Recovery, rehabilitation and resilient reconstruction.

Family Name: Communication from the Commission on Integrated Wildfire Risk Management
Family Summary: The European Commission's 2026 communication on integrated wildfire risk management outlines a holistic strategy to address the escalating threat of wildfires, which saw over 1 million hectares burned in the EU in 2025. The strategy shifts from traditional firefighting toward an "integrated" approach covering the entire disaster cycle: prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery.The communication identifies three main factors driving the surge in extreme "megafires": climate change (extreme heat and droughts), land management changes (abandoned rural areas leading to fuel build-up), and human behavior (responsible for up to 96% of ignitions through negligence or arson).

Family Name: The Building Regulations etc. (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2026 ("Future Homes and Buildings Standards")
Family Summary:
These Regulations were introduced by the government as a statutory instrument authorised by the Buildings Act of 1984. They replace the previous Buildings Regulations for 2010 which introduced requirements for energy efficiency in buildings. The 2010 Regulations were subject to amendments in 2013 and 2021.

The 2026 Regulations - often referred to as the Future Homes and Buildings Standards - require all new dwellings in the UK to meet certain standards which would avoid the need to retrofit them once the grid becomes zero carbon. The standards effectively prevent the use of gas boilers in new builds.

The Regulations were laid before parliament on 24th March 2026. However, they do not enter into force until 24 March 2027, with certain provisions for higher risk buildings not coming fully into force under 24 September 2027, subject to transitional provisions.

Family Name: 15th Five-Year Plan
Family Summary:
China’s 15th Five-Year Plan charts the path for China’s economic and social development for 2026 to 2030. The plan was released and adopted by the National People’s Congress in March 2026. While the previous 14th Five-Year Plan reiterated the previously announced targets of achieving emissions peaking by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060, the 15th Five-Year Plan has more references to emissions peaking than to carbon neutrality, and does not mention any target years.

Chapter III Main Objectives

The main objectives of the 15th Five-Year Plan are listed in Chapter III. The climate-related objectives are to achieve the goal of carbon peaking as scheduled, to reduce the carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 17% by 2030, and to build a clean, low-carbon, safe and efficient new energy system.

Chapter VIII Accelerate the comprehensive green transformation of economic and social development and build a beautiful China

The main provisions concerning climate are in Chapter 13, Article 47.

The chapeau paragraph in Chapter VIII calls for the establishment and practise of the concept of ecological civilisation. To achieve carbon peaking and neutrality, China will promote carbon reduction, pollution reduction, green expansion and growth, improve the quality of the ecological environment, build a strong ecological safety barrier, and enhance the momentum of green development.

Article 47 - Actively and steadily promote and achieve carbon peaking

Section 1: Fully implement the double control of total carbon emissions and emissions intensity

Article 47.1 states that to control total carbon emissions and emissions intensity, China will:

  • Establish a comprehensive evaluation and assessment system for carbon peaking and carbon neutrality;
  • Establish an industry carbon emission control mechanism, clarifying the requirements for carbon emission management in key industries and promoting production capacity management and carbon emission control;
  • Strengthen the energy-saving review and carbon emission evaluation of fixed asset investment projects, and implement the replacement of carbon emissions equivalent or reduced in new and reconstruction and expansion of high-energy-consuming and high-emission industrial projects;
  • Formulate product carbon footprint accounting rules and standards, issue carbon emission limit standards for key products, and establish a product carbon identification certification system;
  • Improve the statistical accounting system of carbon emissions and the dynamic monitoring and early warning mechanism, and normalise the preparation of the national greenhouse gas list; and
  • Expand the coverage of the national carbon emission rights trading market and accelerate the construction of a voluntary greenhouse gas emission reduction trading market.

Section 2: Promote energy conservation and carbon reduction in key areas

Article 47.2 states that China will:

  • Promote coal and oil consumption to peak;
  • Reduce the energy consumption per unit of GDP by about 10%;
  • Accelerate the innovative application of green low-carbon technology and equipment, and build zero-carbon factories and parks.
  • Strengthen the energy-saving and carbon-reducing transformation of existing buildings and municipal facilities, and refrigeration and lighting;
  • Utilise residual heat resources and non-fossil energy heating, and promote the metering transformation of heating;
  • Promote the low-carbon replacement of different modes of transportation and freight; and
  • Improve the energy efficiency of computing facilities.

Section 3: Improve the ability to cope with global climate change

Article 47.3 states that China will:

  • Strengthen the monitoring and control of non-carbon dioxide greenhouse gases;
  • Increase carbon sinks in ecosystems, and improve the monitoring and accounting system of carbon sinks;
  • Improve the work system of adapting to climate change, strengthen the assessment of the impact of regional risks of climate change on key vulnerable areas, and improve the ability to cope with climate change, especially extreme weather; and
  • Actively participate in and lead global climate governance, adhere to the principle of common but differentiated responsibility, fully implement the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and its Paris Agreement, and deepen South-South cooperation on climate change.

Targets

The targets related to carbon peaking and carbon neutrality, as indicated in Table 20 in Article 47, are:

  • Increase the transformation of energy saving in key industries such as thermal power, iron and steel, non-ferrous metals, petrochemical, chemical and building industries, achieve energy savings for more than 150 million tons of standard coal, and reduce the energy consumption of public institutions by 5%.
  • Build demonstration projects and promote the replacement of coal consumption in food, textile, paper-making and other industries to reach 30 million tons/year.
  • Build about 100 national zero-carbon parks to manufacture green products with green energy, with zero-carbon transportation corridors.
  • Implement non-carbon dioxide greenhouse gas control projects such as for methane, nitrous oxide and hydrofluorocarbons in coal mining, agriculture, waste, chemical and other sectors, reducing carbon dioxide equivalent emissions by 30 million tons.
  • Build a comprehensive national carbon emissions data management system, a national greenhouse emissions factor database and a national carbon measurement laboratory.
  • Support the innovation of carbon dioxide capture and bio-dissipation, and support the construction of carbon capture, utilisation and sequestration demonstration projects.

Other relevant provisions in Chapter 13 are as follows:

Article 48 - Continuous improvement of environmental quality

Family Name: Land Use Framework
Family Summary:
The Land Use Framework for England claims that there is enough land to deliver housing, food production, clean energy and nature recovery together, provided land is used more multifunctionally and decisions are better coordinated. It sets out a 2030 and 2050 vision, four principles for land use decisions (multifunctionality, right use in the right place, future-ready decisions and adaptive design), and actions on spatial planning, data, incentives and shared stewardship. It informs decisions rather than prescribing land uses or forming part of planning policy.

On climate, the framework points to rising risk: about one in four properties in England could face flooding by 2050 under a high-emissions scenario, and recent heatwaves and floods have already hit farmland. Its mitigation focus is on nature-based solutions and clean power. Peatlands are described as England's largest terrestrial carbon stores. It envisions woodland cover reaching 16.5% by 2050, more agroforestry, and riverside woodland that also reduces flood risk. It expects at least 95% clean power by 2030, with solar and wind staying around 1% of England's land and often combined with grazing or farming On adaptation, it promises a long-term assessment of climate impacts on land use under 2°C and 4°C scenarios, feeding into the fourth National Adaptation Programme in 2028 and the design of ELM schemes.

Family Name: Whole of Government Circular Economy Strategy 2026-2028: Accelerating Action
Family Summary:
This Strategy is intended to contribute towards Ireland's commitment to net zero by 2050. It contains sections on governance, the construction, bioeconomy, retail, packaging, textile, electronics and electronic equipment sectors, and cross-cutting measures. There are sectoral targets as mandated by the Circular Economy and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2022. One of the targets for this Strategy is to have high-level governance on circular economy represented via the Climate Action Programme Board and the SOG on Climate and the Environment.

In parrticular, development of the bioeconomy including agri-food innovation, carbon farming and biogenic carbon sinks, and the increased sustainability of construction materials are intended to support climate goals.

Climate Act 423/2022 establishes the statutory framework for Finland’s climate policy planning, implementation and monitoring. It sets targets for carbon neutrality by 2035 and greenhouse-gas emission reductions of at least 60% by 2030, 80% by 2040 and 90% by 2050, with a 95% target to be pursued if possible. 
The Act requires a Long-Term Climate Plan, Medium-Term Climate Plan, National Climate Change Adaptation Plan and Land Use Sector Climate Plan.
Family Name: Long-Term Climate Plan (2026)
Family Summary: The Long-Term Climate Plan, prepared under the Climate Act, assesses how possible societal and technological developments could affect Finland’s future greenhouse-gas emissions and carbon sinks and provides a basis for long-term climate and energy policy. It presents 30-year scenarios covering the effort-sharing, emissions-trading and land-use sectors, as well as sector-specific pathways for reducing emissions and increasing removals. The scenarios indicate that Finland could achieve carbon neutrality after 2040 and carbon negativity by mid-century, provided that all major sectors—including industry, energy, transport, agriculture and land use—contribute to the transition. However, developments in forest use and carbon sinks remain highly uncertain. The plan does not itself introduce new policy measures or select a preferred scenario; more detailed policy measures are set out through the National Energy and Climate Strategy, Medium-Term Climate Plan and Climate Plan for the Land Use Sector.

Family Summary:
This Strategy aims to guarantee healthy, sustainable, and accessible food for all by 2030, based on an interministerial approach. Its goal is to build a sustainable food system that ensures food security and nutrition for all without compromising the economic, social, and environmental foundations necessary to guarantee food security and nutrition for future generations.

The four key areas are:

  1. Ensuring coordinated governance of policies related to food, health and the environment at all levels and act at the territorial level;
  2. Guaranteeing access for all to quality and sustainable food and nutrition environments;
  3. Supporting sustainable and healthy and environmentally friendly behaviors and diets; and
  4. Developing research, expertise and evaluation for a transition of food systems.

Family Summary: The strategic plan guides the long-term management of Uganda's wetland resources, securing and enhancing their role in supporting livelihoods, biodiversity, ecosystem services and carbon storage. It supports the Vision 2040 goal to achieve/maintain 13% of the land surface area as wetland by 2040, and acts at the national, subnational and community level to ensure integrated awareness, effective governance and enforcement of sustainable wetland management. The plan seeks to mobilise both local and international finance, and develop natural capital accounts through mapping and inventory research.

This Resolution sets out the results of implementing the Resolution of the previous 13th Congress, and sets out the vision and development orientation for the coming years.

In relation to climate change, the Resolution states that such issues like climate change, traditional security, and non-traditional security have become increasingly complex. The national development orientation for the period 2026-2030, key tasks and strategic actions, therefore, include the following:

  • Manage and develop the society in a sustainable manner; ensure social progress and fairness, and take care of people's lives. Improve the model, mechanisms, and policies for governing and developing a modern, comprehensive, inclusive, and sustainable society; combine economic growth with ensuring social progress and fairness, protecting the environment and natural resources, and proactively adapting to climate change. Develop a rational social structure based on the system of social values and standards. Encourage creative models and approaches in governing and developing sustainable communities.

Synchronise laws, mechanisms, policies and planning schemes for general management and use of natural resources, for environmental protection, and nature and biodiversity conservation; prevent biodiversity degradation, maintain ecological balance. Family Name: National plan for coastal protection of Denmark (Climate Adaptation Plan II)
Family Summary:
With the Climate Adaptation Plan II, the government will take greater responsibility for coastal protection in Denmark. The government will create an investment plan for coastal protection that will ensure a strategic and cross-cutting prioritization of coastal protection projects, so that Denmark is better equipped against the threat from the sea. The government will allocate DKK 14.9 billion for the investment plan up to 2040. With that money, Denmark can build dikes, high water walls and other protection along coasts throughout the country, where there is a significant risk of flooding. With the investment plan, the government proposes a new financing model, where the state will assume a significantly greater responsibility for financing and thus support the municipalities' prioritization of coastal protection.

As part of the further work, a decision must be made on how large a share of the state expenses that landowners will subsequently be charged. The government has set up an expert group to distribute a possible financial contribution to the construction of coastal protection between the landowners, including citizens, businesses and infrastructure owners who obtain protection for the projects. At the same time, the state will take the initiative to initiate feasibility studies as a supplement to municipal feasibility studies. This work has already begun with the acceleration package, where feasibility studies will be carried out for Esbjerg, Kerteminde, Korsør, Vejle and the section from Risskov to Egå near Aarhus in 2026.

Family Summary: The Cabinet Order 85/2026 approved the Plan for reducing emissions of fine particles, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, volatile organic compounds and sulfur dioxide for 2026-2030. The overall goal of the plan is to reduce the negative impact of air pollution on the environment and human health. It tackles the emission of several substances responsible for air pollution, amongst them some greenhouse gases such as SO2 and NOx.The plan makes a clear link between the climate and air protection policies also at the municipal level, where municipalities can voluntarily develop a sustainable energy and climate action plan (SECAP) and outlines measures with a positive impact on air quality, such as the use of emission-free RES (wind, sun) for energy production and measures that increase energy efficiency. Another measure mentioned is the replacement of old and inefficient biomass-using technologies with emission-free renewables also has a positive impact.

Family Summary: The Vision 2035: Critical Minerals Strategy sets out the UK Government’s long-term approach to securing the minerals needed for economic growth and the clean energy transition, recognising their importance for technologies including electric vehicles, wind turbines, batteries and other low-carbon infrastructure. The strategy aims to strengthen domestic production, processing and recycling while diversifying international supply chains, reducing exposure to disruption and supporting a more circular economy. By 2035, the government aims for at least 10% of UK demand for critical minerals to be met through domestic production and 20% through recycling, alongside greater diversification of supply. The strategy also links critical minerals policy to industrial decarbonisation and clean-energy deployment, while emphasising high environmental, social and governance standards in domestic production.

Family Summary: The strategy aims to ensure the sustainable and efficient long-term management of water resources in Belarus, emphasising the need to respond to growing climate-driven threats to water security. It promotes a range of solutions including expanded water storage and irrigation infrastructure, improved flood modelling and ecological approaches such as peatland re-wetting. It also notes methane emission issues from hydropower projects, and the need to balance these concerns against renewable energy benefits, co-ordinating hydropower with landscape-level water management to ensure sustainability. The strategy underscores the need to focus ecological and water quality observation and research on the areas and water systems most vulnerable to climate change.

Family Summary:
This Plan contains goals and actions to ensure energy security in the transition to climate-neutral energy generation with a competitive price by 2050.

(ii) reduction of native vegetation removal through the promotion of conservation and restoration;

Family Name: Energy Efficiency Agreements 2026-2035
Family Summary: Finland's Energy Efficiency Agreements are voluntary schemes—now entering their fourth ten-year cycle (2026–2035), following 1997–2007, 2008–2016, and 2017–2025—through which the government and industry, property, and public-sector organizations jointly meet Finland's binding obligations under the EU Energy Efficiency Directive ((EU) 2023/1791, especially Article 8) without resorting to heavy regulation.The scheme is expected to deliver about 40% of Finland's national energy-saving target for 2021–2030, and the previous 2017–2025 round covered over 60% of Finland's total energy use across nearly 800 companies and 160+ municipalities. The 2026–2035 period is organized into three parallel agreements: Industries (covering energy-intensive industry, food, chemicals, technology, forestry, energy, retail, motor trades, hospitality, and general industry/services, each with its own sector action plan); Public Sector (municipalities, wellbeing services counties, and state entities); and Property Sector (commercial real estate and rental housing, via Rakli). Joining companies set an indicative (non-binding, no-penalty) energy-savings target of 10% by 2035 with a 6% interim target for 2030, based on their own recent baseline energy use, commit to continuous efficiency improvement (via an energy management system such as ISO 50001 or ETJ+, or an equivalent improvement plan) and annual reporting, and in return get access to state investment/audit subsidies, advisory support, a national network, and relief from certain other regulatory obligations.
Document Title: Energy Efficiency Agreement for Industries

Family Name: Program to promote electric cars
Family Summary: The EV support scheme is aimed at private households purchasing or leasing newly registered electric or plug-in hybrid cars from 1 January 2026 onwards. There is a household income cap of €80,000, plus €5,000 per child up to a maximum of two children, i.e. €90,000 in total. The basic funding is capped at €3,000 for EVs, €1,500 for plug-in hybrids and battery electric cars with range extenders. For the latter two, eligibility is only possible if the limit of 60 grams of CO2 per kilometre is met, or if the electric range is at least 80 km. A holding period of 36 months must be observed. For households with an income of up to €60,000, the basic grant increases by €1,000, and for households with an income of up to €45,000, it increases by a further €1,000. An additional €500 is granted for each child, up to two.

Family Name: New energy consumption subsidy scheme
Family Summary:
Argentina has introduced a new, targeted energy subsidy system that replaces the previous income-based segmentation with a unified scheme aimed at households requiring assistance to cover essential energy consumption. The system provides a baseline subsidy of around 50% on a limited “basic consumption block” of electricity and gas, with any consumption above that threshold charged at full cost.

For electricity, the subsidy applies year-round but only up to a capped level of monthly consumption (higher in peak-demand months and lower in milder seasons). For natural gas, subsidies are seasonal, concentrated in winter months (April–September), with no support during periods of low demand.

The scheme also introduces a temporary additional subsidy (up to 25%) during 2026, which gradually declines over the year to ease the transition to higher tariffs.

Family Name: Methodological Guide for the Estimation and Reporting of Greenhouse Gases and Short-Lived Climate Forcers
Family Summary:
Published by Chile's Environmental Assessment Service (SEA) in December 2025, this is the first edition of the Methodological Guide for the Estimation and Reporting of Greenhouse Gases (GHGs) and Short-Lived Climate Forcers (SLCFs). Its publication was prompted by the amendment to the SEIA Regulations under Supreme Decree No. 30 of 2023, which established, as minimum content for Environmental Impact Statements and Studies, the requirement to include "emissions, including greenhouse gases and short-lived climate forcers, from the project or activity and the abatement and control measures contemplated."

The Guide standardises criteria and procedures for estimating GHG and SLCF emissions from projects or activities submitted to the SEIA. It covers stationary and mobile combustion sources, industrial processes, product use, and fugitive emissions. Emissions must be reported in tonnes per year for each project phase and, in the case of GHGs, are also recommended to be expressed in CO₂ equivalent using the IPCC's Global Warming Potentials. The Guide also includes guidance on presenting abatement and control measures.
Document Title: Methodological Guide

Family Name: National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings: 2025
Family Summary:
The National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings: 2025 (NECB) sets technical requirements that address the protection of the environment in the design and construction of new buildings and in subsequent alterations. The 2025 edition of the NECB includes the following updates:

  • Expansion of the environment objective to address greenhouse gas emissions;
  • Introduction of a harmonised framework that aims to reduce the operational greenhouse gas emissions of buildings, offering provinces and territories a harmonised pathway to reduce emissions over time by choosing the performance level that best suits their needs;
  • Introduction of energy efficiency requirements for the alteration of existing buildings, offering building officials a harmonized framework to enforce code requirements in retrofits;

It also promotes landscape and ecosystem protection more generally, and improvements to environmental monitoring systems.

Family Name: Climate adaptation strategy for transport
Family Summary: The Climate Adaptation Strategy for Transport sets out how the transport sector will prepare for the impacts of climate change, built around three themes: a systems-based approach, mainstreaming adaptation into decisions, and building a stronger evidence base. It focuses on England and is a direction of travel rather than a full set of solutions. On climate, the strategy stresses that extreme weather is already disrupting transport, with rails buckling in heat, roads washed out by heavy rain, and ports and airports facing rising disruption. As of 2024, 38% of roads and 37% of railways in England are at risk of flooding, projected to rise to 46% and 54% by 2050. Weather-related incidents cost Network Rail over £1bn in compensation between 2006 and 2021. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates climate damage could cut GDP by 3.2% to 7.8% by 2074, while adaptation measures can return £2 to £10 of benefits per £1 invested.

Family Summary: Finland's National Food Strategy 2040 sets a long-term vision for Finland to become a global leader in sustainable food systems, developed through extensive stakeholder consultation (600+ participants) in response to climate change, geopolitical instability, and biodiversity loss. It is built around four strategic goals: profitability and fairness (raising value-added, fairer income distribution, tripling export value by 2040), security of supply (resilience in critical inputs like nutrients, energy, seeds, and protein feed), nature's carrying capacity (emissions reductions toward carbon neutrality, including peat field emissions, biodiversity restoration, and reduced nutrient runoff), and food culture and wellbeing (healthier diets, food education, sustainable public procurement). Implementation happens through rolling four-year action plans, supported by five cross-cutting capabilities: innovation/technology, skills development, investment capacity, cross-sector cooperation, and a shift toward more enabling public administration — aiming to balance economic competitiveness, ecological limits, and public health by 2040.

2. Expand the availability of and access to healthy food in areas most exposed to climate change.

The Resolution No. 03, dated September 14, 2023, provides for the update of the Climate Plan and defines it as an instrument of the National Policy on Climate Change (PNMC) to consolidate the strategies, plans, and targets of the Federal Executive Branch, contributing to the objectives of the Policy and to the achievement of the targets established in the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) under the Paris Agreement.
Family Name: Brazil's Adaptation Climate Plan: Sectoral Plan for Tourism
Family Summary:
The objectives of the Sectoral Plan for Tourism Adaptation were defined from the perspective of reducing risks to tourism in Brazil caused by the main climate threats and vulnerabilities. Considering that climate impacts can affect multiple dimensions of tourism development, this sectoral plan brings the following goals:

• Sectoral Objective 1. Promote the sustainable development and resilience of tourist destinations through the implementation of climate adaptation practices that strengthen the local ecosystem and foster environmental awareness, as well as the conservation and preservation of environments, generating benefits for tourists and local communities.

• Sectoral Objective 2. Promote climate resilience and safety in Brazilian tourist destinations through integrated adaptation solutions, aiming for sustainable and safe tourism in the face of climate challenges.

• Sectoral Objective 3. Value and contribute to the protection of the lifestyles, traditional knowledge, and cultures of tourism communities dependent on or linked to natural and cultural heritage, with a focus on promoting climate justice.
Document Title: Brazil's Adaptation Climate Plan: Sectoral Plan for Tourism

Family Name: UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2026-2030 Uzbekistan
Family Summary: The co-operation framework comprises an executive-approved strategy for the achievement of the UN's Sustainable Development Goals in the short and medium term. It acknowledges and emphasises the importance of climate change as a threat to wellbeing and economic development, and climate/environment is named as one of six key priority areas. Aside from reinforcing the government's commitment to renewable energy expansion, the framework focuses largely on adaptation measures. It promotes climate-resilient technology and financing systems for the agriculture sector, and a mainstreaming of climate adaptation in health and education systems.
Document Title: UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2026-2030 Uzbekistan

Family Name: Sectoral Adaptation Programme (SAP) on Agriculture 2025-2030
Family Summary: The Sectoral Adaptation Programme (SAP) on Agriculture for 2025-2030 provides a climate vulnerability analysis and recommended actions to ensure effective adaptation to climate change in the agricultural sector. It emphasises issues around water availability and the dependence of the sector on outdated irrigation systems, promoting better surface water collection and storage, covered canals, desalination, crop rotation and the breeding of more stress-tolerant crop varieties. It also promotes broader efforts to build capacity and disseminate information, including integration of agricultural adaptation into education systems and the creation of monitoring systems for soil and air quality. The programme includes an intersection with gender issues, and promotes technical adaptation and better small business infrastructure as tools to mitigate women's heightened vulnerability to climate issues in subsistence farming communities.
Document Title: Sectoral Adaptation Programme (SAP) on Agriculture 2025-2030

Family Name: Landfill Methane Regulations
Family Summary:
These Regulations apply to certain privately and municipally owned landfills that have received municipal solid waste.

These Regulations will reduce methane emissions from landfills through a performance-based approach that sets surface methane concentration limits and requires regular monitoring to confirm these limits are being met and to identify and repair methane leaks.
Document Title: Landfill Methane Regulations (SOR/2025-279)

Family Name: Social Climate Plan
Family Summary:
This Plan addresses the social consequences and key challenges arising from the green transition in Sweden, particularly in the building and transport sectors. This Plan provides an overview of the planned measures and investments for the green transition, and describes measures and the associated costs for electric vehicles, energy efficiency, building renovation, and vulnerable households, amongst other measures.

The Plan will be implemented by the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency. The intention is to use the EU's Social Climate Fund, designed to cushion the impact on those who may struggle the most from increased energy and fuel prices in the context of the EU's Emissions Trading System, to fund these measures.
Document Title: Social Climate Plan

Family Name: Decree No. 12,768, of December 5, 2025 [Decreto nº 12.768, de 5 de dezembro de 2025]
Family Summary:
Decree No. 12,768 establishes the Permanent Technical Advisory Committee (CTCP) as a key institutional body within Brazil’s Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading System (SBCE). The Committee functions as a multi-stakeholder advisory mechanism to support the design, implementation, and continuous improvement of Brazil’s national carbon market framework.

Core functions of the CTCP

• Support implementation and operation of the emissions trading system

• Provide technical recommendations and policy inputs

• Advises on system improvements, methodologies for Verified Emission Reduction or Removal Certificates [Certificado de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVE)], National Allocation Plan criteria and annual allocation planning.

Institutional Positioning

• The Committee is an advisory (non-decision-making) body.

• Reports to and supports the Interministerial Committee on Climate Change [Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima (CIM)] and the SBCE management body.

• Ensures technical grounding of regulatory decisions in the carbon market.

Composition and Representation

A broad, multi-stakeholder structure, including:

• Federal Government (core representation): One representative from each Ministry and one from the Securities and Exchange Commission.

• Subnational governments: 5 representatives from States and Federal District

• Non-state actors: One representative from academia (scientific expertise), one from civil society (national-level representation), one private sector representatives from each sector (energy, industry, transport and mobility, waste and AFOLU), and one from financial institutions.

• Members are appointed by the Minister of Finance.

• Non-government representatives will be selected via public process and will serve 2-year terms.

Governance and Functioning

• Chair: Ministry of Finance

• Meetings: Ordinary (every 2 months) and extraordinary (as needed).

• Chair may take urgent decisions (ad referendum) subject to later validation

Thematic Working Groups

• Committee may establish specialized working groups to address technical or sector-specific issues.

• Limit up to 4 groups simultaneously with a maximum duration of 1 year (renewable)

Regulatory Affairs Chamber

• Dedicated chamber composed of regulated sector representatives, regulated separately by the Ministry of Finance.

• The role fo the Chamber is to provide formal opinions during consultations and hearings.
Document Title: Decree No. 12,768, of December 5, 2025 [Decreto nº 12.768, de 5 de dezembro de 2025]

Collection Summary:
Climate Act 423/2022 establishes the statutory framework for Finland’s climate policy planning, implementation and monitoring. It sets targets for carbon neutrality by 2035 and greenhouse-gas emission reductions of at least 60% by 2030, 80% by 2040 and 90% by 2050, with a 95% target to be pursued if possible. 
The Act requires a Long-Term Climate Plan, Medium-Term Climate Plan, National Climate Change Adaptation Plan and Land Use Sector Climate Plan.
Family Name: Medium-term Climate Change Policy Plan 2025
Family Summary: The Climate Act requires the preparation of the Medium-Term Climate Plan, which focuses on reducing emissions in the effort-sharing sector, including transport, agriculture, building heating, machinery, waste management, F-gases, and industrial activities outside the EU Emissions Trading System. The 2025 plan supports Finland's EU and national climate targets, including a 50% reduction in effort-sharing emissions by 2030 compared with 2005 levels and climate neutrality by 2035. It introduces additional measures expected to deliver at least 0.9 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emission reductions by 2030, including support for low-carbon transport, the phase-out of oil heating, electrification of machinery, renewable fuels, carbon capture in waste incineration, and measures in agriculture. The plan combines sector-specific and cross-cutting measures and is based on statistical analysis and emissions scenarios.
Document Title: Medium-term Climate Change Policy Plan 2025

Family Name: Energising Britain: Your voice in our Clean Energy Superpower Mission
Family Summary: Energising Britain: Your Voice in our Clean Energy Superpower Mission is the UK government's public participation strategy for its Clean Energy Superpower Mission (net zero by 2050, clean power by 2030). It sets out how government will engage people and communities in climate and energy policy, built around five principles: Communicate (e.g. a new Clean Energy Mission website, Listen (local and regional engagement, citizen assemblies, etc), Enable (addressing practical/financial barriers via schemes like the Electric Car Grant and Boiler Upgrade Scheme), Grow, and Collaborate. It draws on earlier participatory exercises and is explicitly coordinated with parallel engagement strategies from the Scottish and Welsh governments.
Document Title: Energising Britain: Your voice in our Clean Energy Superpower Mission

Family Name: Environmental Improvement Plan 2025
Family Summary:
The Environmental Improvement Plan (EIP) 2025 is a strategic framework for improving England’s natural environment up to 2043, containing interim targets for the statutory Environment Act 2021 targets. It sets out how the government will work alongside individuals, communities and businesses to achieve England's nature ambitions in the context of nature depletion.

The EIP contains 10 goals on: the restoration of nature; the improvement of environmental quality through goals on air, water, chemicals and pesticides; driving forward a circular economy through goals on waste and resources; the achievement of environmental security through goals on climate, hazards and biosecurity; and increase to access to nature.

There is a focus on actions and investment to:

  • enhance the quantity and state of our critical natural capital assets;
  • capture more of the benefits from natural assets; and
  • reduce the pressures on our natural capital assets from direct use and respond to external threats.
Document Title: Environmental Improvement Plan

Family Name: Master Plan 2025
Family Summary:
The Master Plan (MP) is the statutory land use plan which guides Singapore's development in the medium term over the next 10 to 15 years. It is reviewed every five years and translates the broad long-term strategies of the Long-Term Plan into detailed plans to guide the development of land and property. The Master Plan shows the permissible land use and density for developments in Singapore.

One of the themes is strengthening urban resilience, to adapt to the effects of climate change while ensuring the city's liveability and resilience. Singapore is incorporating climate-sensitive urban design strategies across the island and growing its capabilities in urban climate modelling simulation to ensure the city remains liveable in the face of rising heat. Under this theme, Singapore is also enhancing its flood resilience while planning for an adaptable coastline that protects against rising sea levels and exploring underground opportunities to optimise its limited land and build resilient urban infrastructure.

Another theme is enabling sustainable growth, where Singapore will expand its infrastructure capacity to support a vibrant digital economy while achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.
Document Title: Gazette of Master Plan 2025

Family Name: Government Decree 1063/2025 on the handling of equipment containing fluorinated greenhouse gases, ozone-depleting substances or alternative refrigerants
Family Summary: This Decree lays down provisions on fluorinated greenhouse gases, in line with the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/573 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the phase-out of certain substances that deplete the ozone layer, as well as equipment, systems or vehicle air-conditioning systems containing alternative refrigerants, and the qualifications of persons and operators who install, maintain, service, repair, decommission, checks for leaks or carries out the recovery of the aforementioned substances, as well as the equipment required for such operations, the installation certificate and maintenance records.
Document Title: Government Decree 1063/2025 on the handling of equipment containing fluorinated greenhouse gases, ozone-depleting substances or alternative refrigerants

Family Name: National Development Strategy 2 (2026-2030)
Family Summary:
The vision of this Strategy is 'Towards a Prosperous Empowered Upper Middle Income Society by 2030'.

This Strategy sets out national priorities and strategies, including for macro-economic stability, inclusive economic growth, infrastructural development, technology, regional development, social development, international relations and governance. It covers various sectors such as agriculture, mining, manufacturing and tourism. There is a chapter focused on agriculture, food, climate and the environment which covers food security, disaster preparedness, institutional coordination, climate-smart agriculture, and adaptation.

There is also a plan to increase green finance, where the Ministry of Finance, Economic Development Investment Promotion will establish the framework for green finance supported by a comprehensive green taxonomy that clearly defines eligible climate-related investments.
Document Title: National Development Strategy 2 (2026-2030)

Family Name: Debt Guarantee Order on Renewable Energy Investment, S.I. 86 of 2025
Family Summary: The Debt Guarantee Order on Renewable Energy Investment, S.I. 86 of 2025, makes the Seychelles government guarantor for a a development loan from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development to the Seychelles Public Utilities Corporation, the main parastatal electricity provider, promoting a USD $8,000,000 investment in grid upgrades for significant expansion of renewable energy generation.
Document Title: Debt Guarantee Order on Renewable Energy Investment, S.I. 86 of 2025

Family Name: Sectoral Adaptation Plan - Electricity and Gas Networks
Family Summary:
The 2024 National Adaptation Framework (NAF) requires the development of Sectoral Adaptation Plans (SAPs) for 13 key sectors. The SAPs were developed applying a six-step adaptation planning process described in Sectoral Planning Guidelines for Climate Change Adaptation to prepare the ground, conduct a climate impact screening, prioritise impacts, conduct a detailed climate risk assessment, develop goals, objectives and actions, and establish governance and implementation frameworks.

The goals of the Sectoral Adaptation Plan - Electricity and Gas Networks (EGN) are to:

  • Establish structures to strengthen and enable action across the EGN sector to increase resilience – these include governance structures, stakeholder engagement, reporting mechanisms, and coordination across sectors and subsectors;
  • Strengthen the capacity of the EGN sector to ensure long-term resilience by strengthening the evidence and knowledge base to support proactive adaptation planning; and
  • Deliver a sustainable and resilient EGN sector while avoiding maladaptation and ensuring just resilience.

Examples of actions include:

  • Defining additional indicators to enhance monitoring of EGN sector resilience to weather extremes;
  • Price Review / Price Control mechanisms that continue to require a section on resilience;
  • Review outcomes of the national Review of Response to Storm Éowyn when published, and track progress of any recommended measures.
Document Title: Sectoral Adaptation Plan - Electricity and Gas Networks

Family Name: Roadmap for Carbon Pricing Instruments and Carbon Markets 2025
Family Summary: This roadmap sets out a comprehensive framework for the implementation of carbon pricing instruments and carbon markets in Chile, with the primary aim of contributing to long-term national climate mitigation goals. It follows from provisions in Chile's 2022 framework law on climate change, as well as the Paris Agreement of 2015. It promotes both green taxes and carbon trading, and gives aims and criteria for assessment and spending for the money raised across sectors, applying to industrial, transport, land-use, energy storage and waste-related activities. Projects generating carbon certifications are only considered if they have received regulatory approval and apply to national territory only.
Document Title: Resolution 8102, approving the Roadmap for Carbon Pricing Instruments and Carbon Markets 2025
